Hasan Foez Siddique with Nurul Islam Matubber and Munshi Mohammad Ali, Advocates—For the Petitioners. 
Dr Rafiqur Rahman with Abdus Salam Mamun and Md Shahiduzzaman, Advocates—For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Sayed (Md) and others ------ Plaintiff-Respondent- Petitioners
vs 
 Fazar Rahman & others ------ Defendant-Appellant-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-5 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 18-6-2006 and 27-6-2006 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy Court, Chittagong, in Other Class Appeal No. 565 of 2005 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree 6-10-2005 and 10-10-2005 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Patiya, Chittagong, in Other Class Suit No. 131 of 1997 preliminarily decreeing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The present plaintiff-respondent-petitioners as plaintiffs filed Other Class Suit being 131 of 1997 before the learned Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Patiya, Chittagong for partition.

3. The short fact of the plaintiffs suit is that the land described in the schedule was finally published in RS Khatian No. 291 in the name of Anu Mia being an owner of the properties. Anu Mia sold 44 decimals of land to Ashu Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs by a registered deed No. 724 dated 31-1-1954 and plaintiff obtained total 581/3 decimals of land and plaintiffs have been owning and possessing the suit land. The defendants have no right, title and interest in claiming the land of the plaintiff. On 19-9-1997 while the defendants denied to partition the suit land from the jote then the cause of action arose and the plaintiffs were constrained to file the instant suit.

4. The defendant Nos. 1-4 by filing written statement contesting the suit, stating, inter alia, that the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest over the suit land. Moreover, deed in question dated 4-2-1954 did not create any title of the plaintiff in the suit land because there is no similarities in between the land in question in schedule No. 1 and the land described in schedule of the deed, the defendants and their predecessor never sold the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs' predecessor, the defendants are possessing the suit land, hence the plaintiffs suit would be dismissed.

5. During the course of trial 2 PWs and 3 DWs were examined by the trial Court. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Patiya, Chittagong after concluding the trial and on consideration of the evidence on record and papers and documents produced and exhibited decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff by his judgment and decree dated 6-10-2005 and 10-10-2005 respectively.

6. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Patiya, Chittagong the defendant preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Chittagong being Other Class Appeal No. 565 of 2005 which was subsequently heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy Court, Chittagong. The learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy Court, Chittagong after hearing the appeal and considering the evidence on record and after perusing the papers, documents and exhibits allowed the appeal and thereby set aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Patiya, Chittagong.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy Court, Chittagong, the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners preferred the instant revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the High Court Division and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Hasan Foez Siddique with Mr Nurul Islam Matubber and Mr Munshi Mohammad Ali, the learned Counsels appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners, submits at the very outset that the learned appellate Court allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court mainly on 3 grounds. 1. The plaintiffs did not bring all the properties and the schedule of Hotchpot. 2. There are several parties in the jote jointly owning and possessing the suit land but they were not made parties, as such, the suit is bad for defect of parties and 3. There are tanks situated in Khatian Nos. 202 and 291 and there are as many as 200 shares in those tanks who were not made parties. The learned appellate Court observed in his judgment that the plaintiff ought to have sought joint possession but the plaintiff did not seek joint possession in the tank in assailing the judgment of the appellate Court. The learned Counsel further submits that this is nothing but a misreading by the learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy Court, Chittagong but, as a matter of fact, the plaintiff sought joint possession in the tanks and drew attention of the Court. The learned Counsel next submits that the properties of Khatian Nos. 202, 291 and 256 were not brought into Hotchpot as because the properties were not disputed, as such, plaintiff did not feel any necessity to bring those properties in the schedule of Hotchpot. There is no legal bar and no suit can fail by reason merely on non-joinder of parties under Order I, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He also submits that the law is also relaxable in a suit for partition that all the joint property should be included in the schedule of properties. The learned Counsel, in support of his contention, relied in the case of Safaruddin vs Fazlul Hug reported in 49 DLR (AD) 151. The learned Counsel finally submits that the lower appellate Court without considering and without applying his judicial mind reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court which is not at all sustainable in law because in the suit for partition the defect of parties and hotchpotch of the partition suit will not defeat the suit. This is a mere technical defect for which the suit will not be defeated. In this connection the learned Counsel referred the case of Rabija Khatun vs Badshah Meah reported in 47 DLR (AD) 511 wherein it has been stated:

"Hotchpotch—Rule of equity—In a case where all the joint properties were not brought into hotchpotch of the partition suit, the omission will not defeat the suit—a rule of equity as opposed to a rule of law shall be applied on the convenience of the parties concerned without causing prejudice to anyone".

9. In concluding his submission, the learned Counsel stated that the lower appellate Court is absolutely wrong and fallacious in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court which is liable to be interfered by this Court hence the Rule should be made absolute.

10. On the other hand, Dr Rafiqur Rahman with Mr Abdus Salam Mamun and Mr Md Shahiduzzaman, the learned Counsels appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-opposite parties, at the very outset submits that whether in a case where the defect of parties and hotchpotch of the schedule of the properties is present a simple partition suit is maintainable or not. Next he submits that the learned trial Court is absolutely wrong and erroneous in determining the necessary parties of a partition suit as well as the joint properties of all the co-sharers in a partition suit and came to a wrong and fallacious finding occasioning failure of justice. The trial Court, without considering the legal implication of a partition suit and without considering the effect of defect of parties and hotchpotch of the schedule in a partition suit, decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff which is manifestly perverse. The learned Counsel in support of his contention referred the case of Nurul Afsar vs Rafiqul Ahmed reported in 51 DLR (AD) 155 wherein it has been held:

"Hotchpotch—If properties are left out in a partition suit it brooks further litigation. It is true that this rule is relaxable. But there are specific situations calling for relaxation."

11. He further submits that the properties of Khatian No. 291 Plot No. 109, the properties of Khatian No. 202 Plot Nos. 124, 125 and 131 and also properties of Khatian No. 256 Plot No. 147 were not brought into hotchpotch and not even in the schedule of the suit properties. He also submits that the plaintiffs sought for Saham of 44 decimal of land in the first schedule as per 1/3 share of his predecessor but, as a matter of fact, as per 1/3 shares the plaintiffs were supposed to get 22 decimals of the suit properties but the trial Court, without calculating the quantum of land merely on the basis of surmise and claim of the plaintiffs, gave Saham of 44 decimals of land and passed the decree in favour of the plaintiff and thereby acted illegally which is liable to be set aside. He further submits that the lower appellate Court was absolutely right and justified in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, inasmuch as not considering the defect of parties and hotchpotch of the suit land. Although the learned Advocate for the petitioner tried to advance his argument that the properties of undisputed khatian and the co-sharer of undisputed khatian if not made parties that will not defeat the suit but, as a matter of fact, this will prejudice other co-sharers. The learned Counsel in support of his contention referred the Case of Mobinnessa vs Khaldur Rahman reported in 37 DLR (AD) 216 which reads as follows:

"In the partition suit five of the appellants, (plaintiff Nos. 1-5) were not impleaded. In a partition suit, the established principle of law is that all co-sharers shall be impleaded and that failure to implead any co-sharer shall render the suit liable for dismissal on the ground of maintainability".

12. The learned Counsel finally submits that so long in this partition suit a serious dispute emerges on the question of quantum of land in the first schedule i.e. the plaintiffs claimed 44 decimal of land as per 1/3 share but according to 1/3 share of the plaintiff, he is entitled to get 22 decimal of land. This vital point of dispute cannot be resolved by a mere partition suit, to determine and to resolve this vital question of dispute the plaintiff must seek remedy in a separate title suit. In this connection, the learned Counsel referred the case of Rezaul Karim vs Shamsuzzoha reported in 49 DLR (AD) 68 wherein it has been stated:

"In a suit for partition the Court will no doubt consider the title of the plaintiffs to the suit land in some detail more than in a suit for permanent injunction, but it cannot in either case convert itself into a Court for determination of the respective titles of the parties if a serious dispute emerges from the pleadings as to the title of the plaintiffs to the partible property and if it is not possible to effect partition without formally determining the plaintiffs' title to the property claimed in the partition suit. Both the Courts below concurrently held, without being reversed by the High Court Division, that the plaintiffs failed to prove settlement of the suit land with their mother Asia Khatun. If the plaintiffs are desirous of getting their full share as claimed in the present suit they must take the responsibility of proving their claim in a full-fledged suit for declaration of title".

13. The lower appellate Court by his judgment and decree dated 18-6-2006 and 27-6-2006 respectively tried to discuss all the legal aspects of the case as well as the factual aspect of the case and also discussed the evidence on record and came to a proper and justified finding in reversing the judgment and decree dated 6-10-2005 and 10-10-2005 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Patiya, Chittagong, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court do not call for any interference by this Court, hence the Rule should be discharged.

<u>14. On a meticulous examination on the evidence on record, papers and documents produced by both the parties and also the legal aspect of the case and the judgment of both the Courts below, it transpires that the learned trial Court was wrong and erroneous in not considering the vital and legal aspects of the case as well as the factual aspects of the case. The trial Court observed in his judgment: "It may be presumed that the plaintiffs perhaps, are in possession in the land as they claimed by Exhibit 3 maintaining their right, title and interest upon it which is manifestly perverse." It may be presumed" and "perhaps"—these words should not be used in drawing legal conclusion and always should avoid surmise and conjecture and presumption. The learned trial Court, on the basis of presumption and surmise without determining and calculating the quantum, gave the Sahan to the plaintiff in first schedule to the extent of 44 decimal of land which is not legally tenable in respect of 1/3 share of plaintiffs' predecessor. On the other hand, the lower appellate Court, considering and determining all the legal and factual aspects of the case, passed the judgment in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court which does not call for any interference by the Court.</u>

15. By now the settled principle of law in exercising the revisional power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been laid down in several judicial pronouncements of our Appellate Division that the finding of facts, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is final unless it is manifestly perverse or vitiated by misreading or non-consideration of material evidence affecting the merit of the case. In this connection I like to rely on the decision in the case of Khurshid Ali vs Noorjahan Bewa reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 82 wherein it has been held that:

"When the appellate Court as the final Court of fact decides questions of fact and records its findings on consideration of the evidence on record, the High Court Division while exercising revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere with findings of fact unless the High Court Division is satisfied that the said findings are perverse. When the material findings of the appellate Court are upheld by the High Court Division and in doing so it commits no error of law, the decision of the High Court Division calls for no interference by the Appellate Division."

16. Another decision can also be cited in the case of Hazari Bala Sana vs Niron alias Nironjan Mondal reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 295 wherein it has been stated that:

"It is a settled principle that the finding of facts, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court, which is the final Court of fact, is binding on the High Court Division, as a revisional Court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case."

17. From the judgment of the lower appellate Court it transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered all the material and legal aspects of the case and the evidence on record both oral and documentary affecting the merit of the case. The learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners also could not point out any error or illegality or infirmity of law in the judgment passed by the lower appellate Court.

18. In view of the discussion made above and the facts and legal position of the case in impugned judgment and decree dated 18-6-2006 and 27-6-2006 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy Court, Chittagong, in Other Class Appeal No. 565 of 2005 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 6-10-2005 and 10-10-2005 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Patiya, in Other Class Suit No. 131 of 1997 and the case having been concluded on finding of law points as well as on facts, no interference is called for in revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

19. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to the costs.

20. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Lower Court's record be sent down forthwith with a copy of the judgment.

End.
